paper_title: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack a human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision a four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for a broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds.

sections.content: World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds Jize Wang 1 2 Yongcheng Jing 2 * Xinyi Le 1 Cailian Chen 1 * Xinping Guan 1 Dacheng Tao 2 * Abstract Emerging Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are moving beyond representation learning towards latent world models that support prediction, planning, and control. Yet their latent worlds naturally lack human-interpretable interface. In this Perspective, we argue that as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. To this end, we envision four-stage research agenda, involving Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act, to guide this shift toward actionable latent-world understanding. Within our framework, existing JEPA interpretability efforts provide early evidence for Ground, while systematic analysis of latent structure, causal verification, and intervention remains largely unexplored. Overall, this Perspective aims to call for broader latent-world interpretability agenda that shifts attention from decoding representations toward understanding, validating, and acting on latent worlds. 1 1. Introduction Learning models that can understand and predict the physical world is long-standing goal of artificial intelligence (Dong et al., 2026; Hafner et al., 2025; Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018). In particular, the emerging JointEmbedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) (Assran et al., 2023; Bardes et al., 2024; 2023; Ghaemi et al., 2026; Skenderi et al., 2025) offer promising approach by predicting 1School of Automation and Intelligent Sensing, Shanghai Jiao Tong University 2College of Computing and Data CorresponScience, Nanyang Technological University. dence to: Yongcheng Jing <yongcheng.jing@ntu.edu.sg>, Cailian Chen <cailianchen@sjtu.edu.cn>, Dacheng Tao <dacheng.tao@gmail.com>. Preprint. October 20, 2026. 1A curated list of related work is available at https://gi thub.com/Jize-W/Awesome-World-Model-Interpr etability. 1 in representation space rather than reconstructing observations at the pixel level. Recent notable developments such as V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026) further extend this idea toward world modeling, where learned latent representations support the prediction of future states and, when conditioned on actions, can be used for planning and control. JEPA-based models have also expanded beyond general-purpose visual representation learning to embodied control and robotics (Sun et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2026), 3D scene understanding (McVay et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026), medical analysis (Liu et al., 2026; Radhachandran et al., 2026; Shah et al., 2025), scientific discovery (Larey et al., 2026; ElSheikh et al., 2026; Bardhan et al., 2025), and other domains (He et al., 2026; Hassan et al., 2026). As JEPAs take on broader roles, their latent spaces increasingly serve as internal states for representing and predicting how the world evolves. This encouraging shift, on the other hand, also raises largely overlooked question: what world has JEPA learned inside its latent space? This question is challenging, because unlike generative world models that produce humanobservable predictions, JEPAs intrinsically predict in an abstract representation space without naturally interpretable interface. When prediction fails, it is therefore difficult to determine whether the failure arises from the represented state, learned dynamics, missing interactions, or errors accumulated over time. More broadly, predictive performance alone cannot establish whether model has learned meaningful world structure or relies on shortcuts that succeed within its training distribution (Kang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). Currently, few existing approaches to representation interpretability provide natural starting point for addressing this problem. They can reveal what semantic or physical information is recoverable from learned representations, such as objects, motion, and actions (Yuan & Søgaard, 2025; Tehenan et al., 2025; Spies et al., 2025). However, decodability alone does not establish how this information participates in the models internal world. Recovering velocity, for example, does not show how it relates to other variables, shapes latent dynamics, or causally contributes to prediction. As such, interpreting latent world model World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds Figure 1. Evolution and positioning of interpretability for latent-space world models. Despite rapid advances in latent-space world modeling and rich XAI toolbox, direct interpretation of learned world models remains sparse. Existing efforts largely focus on latent-content probing or isolated analysis and intervention techniques, leaving systematic understanding of latent worlds underexplored. therefore requires moving beyond what its representations encode toward how they function together as predictive system. To instantiate this point, Figure 1 situates the gap within the broader landscape of world modeling and interpretability. Although general XAI and mechanistic interpretability offer rich toolbox (Sundararajan et al., 2017; Wachter et al., 2017; Alain & Bengio, 2017; Kim et al., 2018; Huben et al., 2024; Olah et al., 2020; Meng et al., 2022; Turner et al., 2023), this toolbox has rarely been applied to learned world models as the primary object of interpretation. Existing XAI studies involving world representations largely pursue different objectives. Some introduce explicit world structure as modeling mechanism: TDB (Dedieu et al., 2024) uses discrete bottlenecks to extract cognitive maps, OOCDM (Yu et al., 2024) builds object-oriented causal dynamics models, and C-JEPA (Nam et al., 2026) introduces object-centric latent structure. Others use world models as an interpretability lens, asking whether Transformers or LLMs develop structured internal representations that resemble world models (Rohekar et al., 2025; Spies et al., In both cases, the learned 2025; Tehenan et al., 2025). world model itself is not the primary object of interpretation. Direct interpretability of learned world models remains scarce. Existing efforts primarily probe what information is encoded in latent representations (Assran et al., 2025; Ming, 2026) or explore individual analysis and intervention techniques (Challagundla et al., 2026; Hong et al., 2026). Consequently, how latent variables are organized, evolve, and causally support prediction remains largely unexplored. Our position is therefore: as JEPA latents become internal states for prediction and action, interpretability must move beyond what they encode to how latent variables interact, evolve, and causally drive prediction. Towards this shift, we envision four-stage blueprint: Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act. Specifically, Ground connects latent factors to variables in the external world. Structure studies how these factors relate and evolve through the models learned dynamics. Verify tests whether the identified factors and structures are causally involved in prediction through controlled interventions. Finally, Act uses this understanding to diagnose failures and improve model behavior. Together, these stages shift the interpretability from identifying information that can be extracted from representations to understanding the internal mechanisms through which latent world model represents, predicts, and acts upon the world. In sum, our contribution is to establish clear formulation of latent-world interpretability for predictive world models and provide systematic blueprint for studying it. We organize existing efforts through this lens, identify the key gaps that remain, and outline how closing these gaps could enable more informative diagnosis, evaluation, and improvement of predictive world models. Finally, we discuss alternative views and identify priorities for advancing this emerging research agenda. 2. Technical Setup 2.1. Despite their methodological differences, these approaches share common question: What information about the world can be decoded from the latent representation? 2.3. The Gap: Decoding Is Not Understanding Decodability establishes that information about world variable is accessible from latent state, but not how it is organized or used by the predictive dynamics. This distinction matters for world models, where latent states are transformed over time to predict how the world evolves. Consider simple example in which velocity can be accurately decoded from zt. This establishes that velocityrelated information is accessible from the representation, but not how velocity relates to other variables such as object position or contact, or how these variables jointly evolve over time. More importantly, successful decoding does not establish that the predictor actually uses velocity-related information when computing ˆzt+1 (Dedieu et al., 2024). The same prediction could instead be driven by correlated visual cues or other shortcuts. We therefore distinguish representational accessibility from world-model understanding. The former concerns what information can be recovered from latent states; the latter concerns how that information is organized, evolves through learned dynamics, and causally contributes to prediction. For action-conditioned models, it also concerns how actions influence this evolution. The next section develops fourstage blueprint for moving toward such understanding. Takeaway 1: Decodability is not understanding. Recovering world variable from latent state shows that the information is accessible, but not how it is organized, how it evolves, or whether the predictor causally relies on it. 3. Blueprint: From Decoding to Understanding Latent Worlds To move from representational accessibility toward worldmodel understanding, we introduce four-stage blueprint: Ground, Structure, Verify, and Act. The stages progressively ask what latent factors correspond to in the external world, how they relate and evolve, whether the model causally relies on them, and how verified understanding can be used to diagnose and improve model behavior. sections.title: Framework
sections.content: From XAI to latent world interpretability. JEPA interpretability builds on broader methodological foundation in explainable AI (XAI) (Mumuni & Mumuni, 2026) and mechanistic interpretability (Zhang et al., 2026). As described in Section 1 and Figure 1, existing methods range from feature attribution (Sundararajan et al., 2017), counterfactual explanations (Wachter et al., 2017), concept analysis (Kim et al., 2018), and probing to feature discovery (Alain & Bengio, 2017), sparse autoencoders (Huben et al., 2024), circuit analysis (Olah et al., 2020), and activation interventions (Meng et al., 2022). These methods provide many of the tools needed to instantiate our framework, particularly the progression from identifying internal features to causally testing and manipulating them. However, latent predictive world models introduce distinct object of interpretation: not only individual internal features, but also the relations and predictive dynamics that organize them into an evolving latent world. Applying existing interpretability tools in this setting therefore requires extending their focus from representations to the predictive system formed by those representations and their dynamics. 5 World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds Table 1. Representative work related to latent-world interpretability, mapped onto the proposed Ground, Structure, Verify, Act blueprint. We focus on work that directly analyzes the representations, dynamics, or causal mechanisms of learned world models, with particular emphasis on JEPAs. explicit coverage; partial coverage; not addressed. Role Model Scope Approach Ground Structure Verify Act Method Method Infrastructure Transferable Method JEPA JEPA JEPA + Non-JEPA Non-JEPA V-JEPA 2 Probing AIM Probing WorldModelLens WAM Steering Latent worlds are domain-dependent. Figure 3 illustrates how the relevant latent world depends on the application domain. In robot manipulation, relevant variables may describe objects, contacts, and motion (Assran et al., 2025; Khazatsky et al., 2024); in 3D localization, objects, positions, and spatial relations become central (McVay et al., 2025; Achlioptas et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020); while medical (Shah et al., 2025; Schoeffmann et al., 2018) and scientific settings (Larey et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2024) involve different domain-specific variables and interactions. For example, in surgical video understanding (Schoeffmann et al., 2018), an interpretable latent world may involve instruments, anatomical structures, their interactions, and the temporal progression of procedural phases. Decoding these concepts individually would not reveal whether the model captures the procedural structure connecting them or relies on clinically relevant factors when predicting subsequent events. The blueprint therefore provides common interpretability framework while allowing the variables, relations, and dynamics under study to be defined by the domain. Early evidence toward latent-world interpretability. Table 1 summarizes the small body of work that is directly related to latent-world interpretability. Within JEPAs, probing in V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., 2025) shows that frozen representations contain information about appearance, motion, and action, while passive discrete probing (Ming, 2026) examines correspondences between physical variations and unsupervised symbolic structure. These studies primarily provide evidence for grounding world-relevant information in JEPA latent spaces. Emerging infrastructure and results from neighboring model classes begin to address later stages of the framework. WorldModelLens (Challagundla et al., 2026) provides infrastructure for probing, attribution, sparse representation analysis, activation patching, and intervention replay across world-model architectures, including JEPAs. Work on World Action Models (Hong et al., 2026) provides complementary precedent from non-JEPA setting, where structured activation patterns are analyzed, dynamically modeled, and manipulated to affect downstream behavior. These developments suggest methodological paths from representational analysis toward causal intervention, although direct evidence in JEPA-based world models remains limited. What remains missing. Existing work covers the proposed framework unevenly. Direct evidence in JEPAs is concentrated primarily at the Ground stage, with some emerging tools for causal analysis and intervention. Systematic study of how grounded variables are organized into relational and dynamical structure, whether that structure causally supports prediction, and how verified mechanisms can guide targeted intervention remains largely open. Takeaway 3: Direct evidence for latent-world interpretability in JEPAs remains sparse. Existing JEPA interpretability is predominantly concentrated at Ground; advancing toward Structure, Verify, and Act represents an underexplored frontier for latent-world interpretability. 5. sections.title: Worlds Enables
sections.content: In this section, we aim to shift the object of interpretation from representations to latent worlds, changing how world models can be analyzed and evaluated. If the internal variables, relations, and dynamics of JEPA can be grounded and causally verified, they can help explain model successes and failures, assess when predictions should be trusted, and guide improvements in model behavior. To achieve this goal, we highlight four implications below. 5.1. Diagnosing where prediction failures arise prediction error alone reveals little about what went wrong inside world model. Consider robot pushing cup near the edge of table. If the model predicts that the cup will remain on the table but it instead falls, several internal failures could produce the same observed error. The latent state may fail to represent that the cup is near the edge (state representation); the predictor may represent the state correctly but fail to capture the dynamics of losing support (dynamics); it may fail to model the interaction among the robot, cup, and table (interaction); or initially correct predictions may drift during multi-step prediction (rollout). Latent world understanding could make these failure modes 6 World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds distinguishable. Grounded factors can reveal whether the relevant state information is present, while recovered relations and transitions can expose where the predicted evolution departs from the expected dynamics. Causal analysis can further identify which internal mechanisms contribute to the failure. Thus, these capabilities could turn interpretability into tool for localizing errors within the predictive process. 5.2. Distinguishing learned world models from shortcuts Strong predictive performance does not necessarily imply that model has captured the underlying structure of the world. Similar performance may arise from meaningful physical structure or from correlated cues such as background texture and camera motion. Latent world interpretability provides way to distinguish these possibilities by examining whether verified internal mechanisms remain predictively relevant as such correlations change. model whose predictions consistently depend on stable world relevant factors across objects, scenes, and environments provides stronger evidence of having captured transferable world structure. Conversely, if prediction depends strongly on factors tied to incidental properties of the training distribution, the apparent world modeling capability may be more fragile than performance suggests. This distinction could provide more informative basis for assessing what kind of world knowledge JEPA has actually acquired. 5.3. Explaining generalization and its limits Understanding latent worlds may also help explain why some predictive models generalize across environments while others fail under distribution shift. Rather than treating generalization only as an empirical property measured on downstream benchmarks, latent world analysis allows us to examine which parts of the internal model remain stable as the environment changes. For example, latent factors that remain stable across changes in object appearance while varying systematically with geometry or dynamics may support transfer across visually different environments (Wang et al., 2025). Conversely, factors that change strongly with background, camera viewpoint, or other task-irrelevant properties may reveal likely sources of out-of-distribution failure (Wang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2024). Studying these invariances and dependencies could connect the internal organization of latent world to the conditions under which its predictions remain reliable (Poudel et al., 2024). Takeaway 4: Similar predictive performance can hide fundamentally different internal worlds. Latent-world analysis can distinguish where failures arise, whether predictions rely on transferable world structure or shortcuts, and which internal mechanisms remain stable under distribution shift. 5.4. From post-hoc explanation to decision-bounded interpretation The consequences of latent world understanding become particularly important when model predictions are used for planning and control. In this setting, an inaccurate internal world can affect not only what the model predicts, but also which actions an agent chooses. Interpretability could provide an additional basis for assessing predictions before they are used for decision making, for example by identifying whether relevant state variables are represented reliably or whether the predicted dynamics are consistent with previously verified mechanisms. This perspective also broadens the role of interpretability in safety. Rather than explaining failures only after an action has been taken, latent world analysis could help assess predictions before they are used for action. For agents that use JEPA predictions for planning and control, interpretability could reveal whether prediction depends on internal variables and dynamics that have been reliably identified and verified, or on patterns known to be unstable under similar conditions. Such information could provide signal for deciding when models prediction should be trusted. 6. Alternative Views and Limitations We consider several alternative views that challenge our position and help clarify its scope. One possible view is that decoding may sometimes be sufficient. This is indeed the case for many interpretability questions. If the goal is to determine whether JEPA representation contains information about object identity, motion, geometry, or another property, well-designed probe may provide all the evidence that is needed. The need for deeper analysis arises when the question concerns the internal predictive world: how represented information is organized, how it participates in prediction, or whether the model causally relies on it. These questions require evidence beyond decodability. Our blueprint is intended for precisely this setting, where representation-level interpretation is useful starting point but not the end of the analysis. deeper concern is whether human-defined variables provide the right ontology for interpreting latent world. JEPA need not decompose its internal computation into familiar concepts such as position, velocity, or contact (Chawla et al., 2026). Its representations may instead be distributed, nonlinear, relational, or task-dependent, and some predictive factors may have no simple humaninterpretable counterpart. Grounding should therefore not presuppose one-to-one correspondence between human concepts and individual neurons or latent directions. Instead, such concepts can serve as reference points for discovering testable correspondences involving subspaces, nonlinear 7 World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds structures, or distributed representations. Cases in which the models internal organization departs from human-defined variables may themselves reveal how it represents the world differently from our chosen description. Another concern is that interventions in latent space may not always be valid. We agree that simply changing latent factor is not sufficient to establish causal relationship. latent representation may encode multiple properties together, so changing factor associated with velocity, for example, could unintentionally change other properties as well. The modified representation may also no longer correspond to plausible state of the world. In either case, change in prediction would be difficult to attribute to the intended intervention. An important challenge for Verify is therefore to develop interventions that change the target factor while preserving other relevant information and keeping the resulting latent state plausible. Determining how to construct and validate such interventions is an important direction for future research. More broadly, interpretability may not be necessary for building reliable world models. Robust prediction and control can also be pursued through behavioral evaluation, uncertainty estimation, robustness training, and outof-distribution testing without examining internal representations. Latent world interpretability should not replace these approaches. Its value is complementary: behavioral evaluation can reveal whether and under what conditions model fails, while internal analysis may help identify the mechanisms behind those failures and distinguish models that achieve similar performance through different internal strategies. This additional evidence may be particularly useful when predictive models are used for planning and control, where prediction failures can directly affect subsequent decisions and actions. Taken together, these considerations highlight important challenges of latent world interpretability. They also clarify where the proposed blueprint applies and where its assumptions and methods require further validation. Takeaway 5: Going beyond decoding does not mean abandoning decoding or behavioral evaluation. Decoding remains sufficient for representation-level questions, while latent-world understanding is needed for claims about predictive mechanisms. Such claims require valid interventions and should complement, rather than replace, behavioral evaluation. 7. Call to Action In aggregate, the aforementioned discussions indicate that realizing latent-world interpretability inevitably requires redirecting research efforts beyond isolated applications of existing interpretability tools toward systematic research program centered on the variables, structures, dynamics, 8 and causal mechanisms of learned worlds. To help shape future research, we highlight four priorities toward this goal. Build controlled testbeds and evaluation criteria. first priority is to develop settings in which latent world interpretations can be tested against known properties of the world. Environments with known objects, physical variables, interactions, and dynamics provide basis for evaluating whether recovered latent structure reflects the underlying system. Evaluation should go beyond decoding accuracy to test whether interpretations remain stable across contexts, whether recovered relations and dynamics are consistent with observed behavior, and whether causal claims hold under controlled changes. Such testbeds will not capture the full complexity of real-world prediction, but they can provide foundation for evaluating latent world interpretations systematically. Study how latent worlds emerge and differ across models. Latent world interpretability should examine how internal predictive structure develops through learning. The organization learned by JEPA may depend on its architecture, training objective, data, model scale, and stage of training (Richens et al., 2025). Comparing models along these dimensions could reveal when world-relevant factors and dynamics begin to emerge, whether similar structures arise across models, and which design choices lead to more stable or reusable internal structure. This would extend interpretability to studying how latent worlds form and evolve. Connect interpretation to model behavior and design. Interpretations should be tested against meaningful differences in prediction, generalization, failure modes, and downstream planning or control. Such connections can also inform model design. If particular internal structures are consistently associated with more reliable prediction or better generalization, they may provide useful evidence for comparing architectures, training objectives, or other design choices. Interpretability could thereby serve not only to analyze trained models, but also to understand which design choices lead to better predictive world models. Scale latent world analysis to realistic settings. Methods developed in controlled environments must eventually be tested on natural video, long-horizon prediction, and embodied agents operating in complex environments. Doing so will require tools for extracting and comparing internal states, tracing predictive computation over time, performing controlled interventions, and analyzing rollouts across model families. Shared infrastructure and evaluation protocols could make these analyses more reproducible and make it easier to compare findings across models and studies. World Model Interpretability: From Decoding Representations to Understanding Latent Worlds 8. Conclusion This Perspective aims to establish latent-world understanding as central goal for interpreting predictive world models. We note that decodability is not understanding: accessible information does not reveal how it is organized, evolves, or causally supports prediction. Building on this observation, we envision the GroundStructureVerifyAct blueprint as path toward this goal, and as framework for shaping future research on latent-world interpretability. We call for future interpretability efforts to move beyond isolated representation-level analyses toward systematically understanding, validating, and acting on the internal worlds learned by predictive models.
